stem.en: Only a few plants of a rare medicinal herb are left in a forest. Scientists want many new plants quickly, without waiting for seeds. They can take small pieces of living tissue from the plants. Which method uses totipotency to do this?

text.en: Grafting the pieces onto a related plant, so that each piece goes on growing on that plant's roots.

feedback.en: No. Grafting keeps a piece growing on another plant, but it does not turn one piece into many new plants.

text.en: Cross-pollinating the few plants that are left, so that they make a larger number of seeds.

feedback.en: No. This still depends on seeds, and the scientists do not want to wait for seeds.

text.en: Keeping the pieces cold in a store until the forest is a safe place for the plant again.

feedback.en: No. Cold storage keeps the pieces, but it makes no new plants.

text.en: Tissue culture: growing living cells from the pieces in a nutrient medium into whole plants.

feedback.en: Yes. Each living piece gives many cells, and totipotent cells can each grow into a new plant.

explanation.en: Steward's carrot experiment showed that living plant cells can be totipotent. So a few small pieces of living tissue hold many possible plants, if the cells are grown in a nutrient medium in the right conditions. This method is plant tissue culture, and it is used to raise many plants of a rare species. Grafting, more seeds and cold storage do not turn a few pieces into many plants.

hints.en: What did the carrot experiment show that a single living plant cell can do?
